utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Registrar. The appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, assisted by our case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stefane Bourgon co-counsel, and Alexis Demirdjian, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Mr. Rodney Dixon, assisted by Mr. Nermin Mulalic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on this day the 24th of March, 2005 the Chamber bids good morning to all those present in this courtroom, which is cosier than hall number 3, but unfortunately we don't have the model that we had yesterday, and the maps. But we will do our best to make up for this. So I bid good morning to representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel - I see that one is missing; I hope we will see him next week - the two accused, as well as the General, the expert witness. I do not wish to forget Mr. Registrar, the usher, the legal officer, the court recorders, and all those assisting us. We need to continue our work with the continuation of the examination-in-chief and, for this purpose, I shall give the floor to Mr. Bourgon to continue with his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning Madam Judge, good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning, General. Further to our review yesterday of both the model of Bosnia-Herzegovina and of some of the annexes to your report, I have a number of questions for you this morning. And if at all possible, I would invite you to try and, once again, keep your answers as short as possible where, of course, this is possible for you to do. The first topic I would like to address with you this morning is that of the events in Dusina. Yesterday you did explain to the Trial Chamber for what reason General Hadzihasanovic, a corps commander, was involved in fighting at this level in the Lasva Valley. I refer you to paragraph 677 of your report, and I would ask that you take a look at 677 of your report. In paragraph 677, you explain what, in your opinion, would be expected to take place. And then you say, "in the knowledge of the corps commander and possibly at his initiative." So before we go into each category I would like to -- you to explain what you mean exactly by "In the knowledge of the corps commander and possibly at his initiative." What did you mean by these words?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this paragraph, 677, I wanted to indicate the measures that the 3rd Corps commander should have taken as well as all others in the chain of command in connection with the steps that needed to be taken in connection with the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I will follow up to this question by asking you, when we say "in the knowledge of the corps commander," what are we to understand in terms of measures taken by others in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon learning about a certain criminal act and depending at what level that criminal offence occurred, meaning which level of unit and at which level in the chain of command. Depending on that, the unit and the commander, in whose unit this occurred, in whose area of responsibility this happened, is duty-bound to take the first steps. And briefly I could list those first steps as follows: Having learnt about a certain event, steps need to be taken as quickly as possible to carry out the identification and on-site inspection to learn as much as possible about the event. Then to take steps to protect, secure and possibly halt the continuation of this adverse event. If it's over, then it's over. But if it is still underway, it has to be stopped and its continuation prevented. That same commander, at a certain level, needs to take measures to report to his superiors up the chain of command. With the assistance of his security service and his military police, he needs to take measures once he has learned the facts of the event in order to institute criminal proceedings. After that, it is the duty and obligation of the commander to prevent the possibility of such events being repeated. How? By issuing orders to his subordinates down the chain of command; by learning a lesson from the event of the event that has already taken place, so that nothing like it could be repeated; making it quite clear that such things would not be tolerated in the future either. Also taking measures to educate and train people, as far as possibilities allow, and providing certain instructions and guidelines additionally and, again, regardless of how many times the commander may have issued such instructions down the chain of command to his subordinates, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My next question deals with, or relates to what you said yesterday about the level at which the corps commander exercises his duty. And my question to you is: When an event like this occurs, is it more likely that the measures will be taken at various levels within the chain of command, or that the corps commander will take such measures himself?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In answer to your previous question, I think I have already answered that question in part. An event, a criminal event, if it occurs in a battalion, in a brigade, an operations group, or at the corps command, at whatever level, so each commander at those levels has the duty to take steps first, together with all his services and bodies that he has at his disposal. And then to undertake all the other steps that I have just listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would like now to ask you a question or for your opinion on an answer which was provided by General Cordy-Simpson, whom I mentioned yesterday. The following question was put to him. In your view, General, what should a corps commander do to prevent violations from happening, bearing in mind what you just said as to what he can and cannot do. And his answers was -- his answer was he can only lay down to his battalion commanders or, in the case of a corps commander, to his divisional commander and his brigade commanders how he wishes operations to be conducted and on what sort of code of behavior. Having passed that information, he must either expect that his subordinates will carry out his orders, or if he finds subsequently that they haven't carried out his orders, then he must order an investigation into why that has not happened. But he cannot influence the individual actions of soldiers on the ground at a particular moment in time. Do you agree with this answer provided General Cordy-Simpson, and can you provide your opinion on this topic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the greatest extent I agree with the answer given by General Simpson, namely, each commander, at whatever level, has the possibility of command and control over units and dealing with problems that occur in the units exclusively along the chain of command. He has no other possibility. Therefore every commander must trust his staff in his chain of command. If that is lacking, it is impossible to run a unit and such a unit would soon fail. It could not function at all. Each commander, and especially at higher levels, at operative levels, is too far removed from a group of soldiers to be able to control what a single soldier or a group of soldiers are doing. He's so far removed that even if he wanted to have control over each and every soldier, in a corps numbering 40.000 men, or my corps which had more than 75.000 men he just couldn't do it. That is not [Realtime transcript read in error "now"] how control and command function. Every commander - I will repeat again what I said in my previous answer - has the task and duty to pass on all the orders and instructions he receives from a superior command or those that he himself issues to forward them down to the lowest level within the structure of his unit and he must daily place emphasis on those matters because every military unit is a living organism and it has to be urged from one day to the next, to consistently implement all those regulations and rules and practice. And they must be told that no deviation will be tolerated. And as soon as the commander becomes aware of a violation, sanctions will be enforced.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would like just to make a correction to the transcript on page 6, line 3, where the transcript reads "that is now how control and command function". My understanding is that what you said was "that is not how control and command function". Can you confirm?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, you mentioned a few minutes ago the existence of operational groups. And this brings the following question: How many levels down is an officer or commanding officer, from a structural point of view, how many levels down is he expected to have contacts with his subordinates in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand. What level are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry. I will make my question more precise. If I take the commander at the corps level, how many levels down from the corps is he expected to have contacts with his subordinate? Is it one level, just the operational group? Would it be two levels, operational group and brigade. Would it be three levels, operational group, brigade, and battalion? To your experience, as a corps commander, how many levels down are you expected to have contacts with your subordinate commanding officers?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: How many levels there are in a corps, as in operative unit, is that the question? The corps level. The next level is the operative brigades level. The third lower level are the brigades. The fourth level down are battalions. The fifth level are companies. The sixth are platoons and the seventh are squads. And then the eighth level is the soldier, the private. Those are the levels. The corps commander has the duty of having contact with his immediate subordinate and those are the assistants in his own corps command and the commanders of units that are directly on the line with the corps commander. In his corps command, on an average, he has eight to ten assistants. And as many unit commanders as we saw on one of the charts of the structure of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH. I can give you my own example. In the course of 1993, I had more than 30 connections. To me, this is beyond the number envisaged by any military theory and doctrine, including foreign military doctrines from one state to another. The maximum connection that one commander should have would be five to seven. The maximum being up to ten. I had 30, and I believe that the 3rd Corps commander must have had 20, if not more. I don't know whether I answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, General. As a follow up to that, first I must ask you, are you familiar with the testimony of General Reinhardt who was the Prosecution expert in this case?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In response to a question put to him, General Reinhardt said that the fact that General Hadzihasanovic created operational groups to reduce the number of people or subordinate commanders answering directly to him, General Reinhardt said that this was a very clever commander. Can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely the question stemming from my previous answer. Namely, the gentleman said that the 3rd Corps commander was a very wise and clever man, for the simple reason that military theory does not allow a commander, especially a senior commander, to have a large number of connections. Not just the higher level commander. So this requires reducing the number of those connections in the formation of operative groups and this is something that he welcomed. And these were formed with one single aim in mind, to reduce the number of connections, to reduce the number of people reporting directly to the corps commander, so that he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would be more operational, successful and effective in his mission. And he noted that very well. And I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I move on to the event of Dusina itself. And in the event of Dusina itself, as you know, there were a series of reports, combat reports from various level on the ground, which were forwarded to the corps headquarters. My question to you is: Did General Hadzihasanovic, and his deputy, General Merdan, give proper consideration to those reports and how important would those reports have been to you, in a similar situation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reviewing all the documents I had access to, I can provide the following answer. All the documents that arrived to the 3rd Corps in those days, the Municipal and District Staff of defence of Zenica were exchanged and all of them were disclosed that very moment, or rather forwarded up the chain of command so that information was given to others who were entitled to having such information so as to deal with the problem and to take appropriate measures. Having reviewed not just this event in Dusina, but all the events, and on the basis of all the documents and information I had, my answer would be to say that I never noticed, in any document that there may have been subconscious -- a subconscious event to avoid the truth about the event, not to mention to conceal the truth about those events. The fact that in some cases the response differed from one to another, I am deeply convinced, on the basis of my own experience, that this was due simply to the lack of relevant information at a given point of time, and the lack of proper information and lack of control over the situation at a given moment. Regarding the event itself and all the information about the event, and informing all entities about the event, which is very important for all -- for the most effective measures to be taken in response. But this, again, is a problem resulting from many other shortcomings and omissions typical of that time period about which I could have much to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You mentioned something rather interesting, in the sense of -- that there was no -- you mentioned -- I will try to use your exact words: "A subconscious event to avoid the truth" and that there was "not to mention to conceal the truth about these events." Now, General, my question to you is: Isn't that the basis for the trust relationship that must exist in a chain of command whereby the commander of the army expects that what he receive from General Hadzihasanovic would be, to the best of his knowledge, the situation on the ground, as General Hadzihasanovic would expect to receive information from his subordinates which would reflect the situation on the ground to the best of their ability?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that is the only way and I would say the only possible way. Even if the commander wanted, through other channels and other ways to learn about certain events, in the given circumstances, he didn't have any such chance to do that. So I repeat what I have already said. The only thing the commander can rely on is his own chain of command. Everything he receives from below is his only source. Whatever it may be, he must take it as being a relevant source. But every commander at whatever level is entitled to verify the source, to check out the source. But even that checking, which may be made at any point in time and regarding any event, must, again, be done through the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you look at footnote 134 in your report. And I believe footnote 134 refers to one of the steps which may be taken. Now, this step is "If the allegations are founded, ensure that measures will be taken by the appropriate subordinate commander, which would normally be the filing of a criminal report before the District Military Prosecutor." This takes us to footnote 134, where you say that: "Concerning the filing of criminal reports, these reports can be done by the military police, whether at the brigade, operational group or corps level." So that is my first question, the levels at which criminal reports may be filed. And the second question is, you say that once a criminal report has been filed, the obligations of the commander are limited to providing assistance to the competent authorities, if requested to do so. Can you provide or confirm that this is still your -- those are still your views today?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. A corps commander, as you have said, when he establishes within the chain of command that an offence has been committed, that there has been a criminal act, regardless of who institutes criminal proceedings, certain relevant facts are established as a result of which criminal proceedings are instituted. In such a procedure, the commanders have a lot of obligations and you can't exclude a corps commander. But once a criminal report has been forwarded to the District Military Prosecutor, from that point in time the corps commander is only duty bound in the sense that his military police and security service must be at the service of the District Military Prosecutor, or the court. When it comes to further dealing with the case -- well I wouldn't say the corps commander shouldn't attach an importance to this, but from the time that criminal proceedings are instituted, from the time that Prosecution takes over the case or the district military court then the corps commander no longer has to deal with this. He has far more important issues to resolve and to deal with on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, General Reinhardt, when testifying, noted that, that "the system of justice," meaning the District Military Prosecutor, and "the district military court were slow," and he gave his opinion that the fact that General Hadzihasanovic complained about the fact that this system was slow showed that this is a commander who cares about discipline and the investigation of possible wrongful acts committed by his subordinates. Would you agree with General Reinhardt in this regard?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knowing General Hadzihasanovic, well that's one factor. But since he was a JNA officer, and attained the highest military rank one can attain in the army - he was a brigade commander in the JNA - any officer, any general who knows anything about the JNA, if you asked any such officer what it meant to become a brigade commander, a commander of a brigade that -- such as the brigade he was in command of in the JNA, your answer would be that he was an extremely conscientious man, a disciplined man, a diligent man, a moral man. And I won't go on to list all of the virtues required because if he hadn't been such a man he wouldn't have been able to be a brigade commander. And I know General Hadzihasanovic from the JNA and he was fully aware of what it meant to conceal, pass over in silence a certain truth and especially the truth about crimes that may have been perpetrated. And he was fully aware of the fact that discipline in a military unit can only be established by respecting all the legal rules and regulations. And that if someone didn't respect the regulations, that person should be punished. And that is why he wanted the District Court to be involved, to deal with cases, to solve cases. He didn't want cases that hadn't been solved to remain and in the field it's the corps commander who suffers the consequences. Cases aren't solved. Soldiers believe that there is no punishment and subconsciously they may still continue to think that they can do whatever they want to do, if I may put it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I absolutely agree with the opinion that you quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My last question with respect to Dusina, General, refers to your conclusion, and we find those at paragraphs 687 and 688 of your report. And my question to you is: When the facts in your report, some of the fact that you note in your report, were mentioned to General Reinhardt, he said that, in his view, the commander had done everything and even more of what he was supposed to do. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like move on to a different section, and I need to ask you a few questions before I begin on the notion of effective control. My first question to you is: What is, in your knowledge and experience, the meaning of the exercise of effective control of a commander over a military unit?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a number of cases or examples of the kind of effective control a certain commander has over a certain military unit. I perhaps will first deal with the first case of effective control. What does it mean to have fully effective control? It means that a certain unit, let's take an example, a brigade, is an organic part of the ABiH 3rd Corps. On the basis of documents, it is integrated, it has its place within the organisational structure of the 3rd Corps. In that case, the brigade is under full, 100 per cent effective control of the 3rd Corps commander. There is another version of effective control. For example, the second kind of effective control would be -- well let me go back to the first version, the corps commander has the right to issue orders. He has the tasks and the mission to support the unit. He has to -- has a right to take disciplinary measures, to punish, et cetera, et cetera. But in the second version of effective control, for example, a central 1st corps brigade and resubordinate it to, let's say, the 3rd Corps. In the second version, what most frequently happens is the brigade that arrives in the 3rd Corps carries out a certain task, during a certain period of time. The 3rd Corps commander usually has the right to command to issue orders to that unit, to support the unit, he has to support the unit. Whereas he doesn't have the right to take disciplinary measures, to punish. He doesn't have the right to change the men, replace the men within the unit who have been temporarily placed under his command. He doesn't have the right to have financial resources at his disposal, because resources, personnel, discipline, these are things that the mother unit remains responsible for. This is what we call resubordination. This is the second kind of effective control, effective control of certain elements, in certain fields but not in all fields, not in all areas. For example, the third kind of effective control is as follows: If a unit comes from another unit and participates in combat and cooperates at the left or right flank of the 3rd Corps, and then the 3rd Corps commander is told that he should give fire support to some other unit that isn't part of his structure, but cooperates with him. And providing fire support is also a kind of effective control, but only in that area. Then in these three versions of effective control commanders at higher levels can have certain other combinations of effective control. The person sending a unit, the person resubordinating it to another unit is -- well, this is in fact something that is regulated in a document, the responsibilities of the original unit are regulated and the rights of the new commander to whom a unit has been resubordinated is also defined and established in documents. I think I have been sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would like to ask for your opinion on a question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, I apologise for interrupting, but the question seems extremely important to me. With regard to a brigade that is temporarily subordinated to the 3rd Corps, that's the example that you provided, you said that the 3rd Corps commander did not have the capability of dealing with questions concerning personnel, discipline, and you said he didn't have financial resources. What article, what text, what document is this based on from the military rules? Was this a matter of practice? Or was it based on specific documents and, in particular, I'm referring to disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case, I would say that it was mostly a matter of practice; however, I'm fully persuaded that there are documents about this in the JNA. I'm not sure whether any of these documents were adopted in the course of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know whether any of these documents from the JNA were adopted. I would need time to find these documents, to see how all of these matters are regulated, but I stand by what I said. All officers would confirm this from the JNA and from ABiH. And most officers from foreign armies would confirm this because the situation is very similar in all armies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, my next question is, I would like to ask you or to ask for your opinion on a question which was put to General Sir Martin Garrod, who was the commander of the Royal marines in the United Kingdom and who testified before this Trial Chamber. The question that was put to you [sic] was as follows: "I would like to ask you something about the subject of control. On a number of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. occasions, in answering questions, you refer to the question of Mujahedin and as to whether they were under control or out of control. As a military man and a very high ranking officer, could you define control. When one has a command over a particular geographic area, how would you define that control?" Sir Martin's answer was as follows: "I would say that the elements of the forces in your area were doing, carrying out your orders and that they knew exactly what they were doing and they were not doing something" - sorry - "anything which was unacceptable to you." Can you comment on this answer by General Sir Martin Garrod?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday we could see on the relief how large the zone of the responsibility of the 3rd Corps was. In the military sense, when you're defining the zone of responsibility of a unit, and I am referring to a corps in this case, you usually take certain prominent features in the land, the tops of those features. And then the line of the zone of responsibility is drawn from one elevation to another elevation, to crossroad, to the following elevation, et cetera, et cetera, and this is how you define the zone of responsibility of, let's say, a corps. I think this is important. The fact that you usually draw a line from one elevation to another elevation. This is important because in military terms, military units are important, military units engaged in combat. Their objective is to take prominent features, elevations, because from such elevations you can monitor the situation, see what the conditions are like. Your position is better than the position of those who are at a lower geographical point. What do I want to say? When you define the zone of a corps, when the area is encircled, this doesn't mean that the corps commander has the task and obligation to deal with all possible problems in the zone of responsibility, whatever the problems may be. That is not the case. That is not the case. In any army anywhere in the world, unless an occupation is to be carried out and you arrive in a new territory, a military occupational system is established, in such cases the unit commander has all the rights, and he is the greatest authority in the territory for the civilians, for the military. He's the supreme authority. In this case, the zone of responsibility, the sort of zones of responsibility that we had in the course of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was such that the corps commander in that zone of responsibility had effective control only over his own units, or rather over the military potential. That was part of the corps. Men, resources, or something else, or perhaps other factors that had an influence on how the daily tasks of the corps were carried out. All other matters were the responsibility of someone else. The corps commander, in legal terms, didn't have any obligations with regard to the civilian population. The corps commander didn't have any obligations or any influence on the civilian police on the civilian police, on the work of the civilian. The corps commander had no influence over the civilian protection, over the bodies of power, municipalities, local communes, cantons, districts, et cetera. So that one shouldn't think that, if you have the zone of responsibility of the corps, everything that happens in that zone of responsibility is something that a corps commander is responsible for. If I may provide you with an example. I do apologise, but in my own case, in the case of Stanislav Galic the Prosecutor put a question to me. I was asked, "Mr. Karavelic, a group of people, at the beginning of 1992 in the summer was in Sarajevo, et cetera." I answered the question and then there was another case, and I said "Well, I apologise, but this has nothing to do with me or with my corps," because this concerned the civilian police and other people. It didn't concern a corps, soldiers. Then I was told, "Mr. Karavelic, if you knew what the responsibility of a commander of a unit in war was, in accordance with international military law, you would never accept such a role." I then explained to him, I said, "Does -- the civilian protection, I had nothing to do with them." There were others and everything that I have just mentioned. And then finally I said, well if I wouldn't have accepted the role of the commander of the 1st Corps to defend Sarajevo I would have accepted different -- someone else would have accepted the role and he would have been in the same situation that I was in, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You mentioned a little earlier various types of forms of subordination. I would like to give you a document and ask you to comment on this document which has to do with forms of subordination, and I have copies for everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just for the record, I don't believe we have seen this document before. And I'm also wondering if my learned colleague can inform us as to who produced this table and what the source of the information contained on the table, where the source material came from for the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President my colleague will see that it is not very complicated. The witness produced it when I met him over the weekend. He could explain the source of the document and he could tell us who produced the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, you will recall that when we met during the weekend, you produced this table for me and I would like you to explain what you meant, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, in terms of forms of subordination. So what this chart illustrates.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It actually illustrates what I have been saying. We have different forms of subordination or effective control. In the top left square, it says "type of subordination, type of control".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can we use the ELMO and put the document ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the top left-hand corner, we have the type of effective control or subordination. And then under "operational command," then under "operational control," there we have the two concepts of command and control, which I will explain later. Then we have, under "control," in the sense of support that I have just spoken about, and then under "control" for administrative support, and the fifth example is in "location." If a support is deployed in a large area and if, in that area or location there are some smaller units coming from other units, that is what this refers to. So in the second heading, going from the left to the right, we have the issuing of orders. And the Xs indicate in which case of control or command orders can be issued. And we know what issuing orders and implementing orders me. Then, in the next column, we have the heading "responsibility for providing support of that command or commander," and again it is marked with Xs, where this is given and where it is not. And in the last column, authority to discipline and to take appropriate measures, where this authority exists and where it doesn't. But I could ask myself, when talking about this second point under "operational control" and discipline, one should distinguish between disciplinary measures and criminal liability. But I would just point out that only if a unit has been resubordinated to another unit and a criminal offence is committed, then the superior is duty-bound to inform the authorities that a criminal offence has been committed for them to be able to process the matter further, that is the commander of the original unit and his superiors can take steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would like to ask you if a few examples so that you can tell us where these examples fit into this chart. And my first question would be: What is the relationship between the HVO an the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina when they are fighting on the same territory and before, of course, they became enemies. What kind of relationship would exist on this chart between the HVO and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this table, the HVO does not exist. And earlier, when speaking about control and the responsibility of the corps commander in his area of responsibility, in his territory, in addition to everything I listed, I omitted to mention a major problem that existed for the 3rd Corps commander in his area. The HVO had his own area and these two areas overlapped. So it is impermissible, and I stand by what I'm saying, that a corps commander in any army in the world would confirm what I'm saying, that the situation, such as it existed in the 3rd Corps, to the effect that within its area of responsibility there was another military structure which also was doing what the 3rd Corps was doing, but as an opponent and as an enemy. And at the same time, the 3rd Corps commander had no authority over them. That is absolutely impermissible according to military doctrine and the theory of war, and one should point out that the 3rd Corps commander was not to blame for this. The political and military top leadership in the state should have, in time, by political means or in some other way, regulated the status of the HVO and they should have prevented the armed conflict that proved to be inevitable after the things that happened and it actually occurred in the summer of 1993. May I just add a sentence? The political and military leadership at the giving was explicit with respect to the Yugoslav People's Army, the Army of Republika Srpska, and the Yugoslav army later on was proclaimed an aggressor. Then the front lines were established the lines of defence and the territory to be defended. So, similarly, the political and military leadership of the state should have much earlier made it clear to the 3rd Corps commander what and how he should act with respect to the Croatian defence council. And they didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The next example I would like you to comment upon is, if we have two armed forces from different states participating into an international operations, for example, Canada and the United States taking part into a NATO operation under command of the United States in Somalia, just to use an example, what would be the relationship between the contingents from Canada and the contingents in the United States, based on your chart, would Canada be under operational command of the United States? Is that possible, or would Canada be under operational control?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, it would most probably be in the second group; that is, under operational control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to move on, General, to your report, the section dealing with the presence of foreigners in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps and I refer specifically to paragraphs 619 to 642 -- sorry, to -- refer to 662. In this section, you describe what a corps commander should do. And that -- I refer to 632 specifically, where you say that: With respect to individuals or groups of individuals who are not under his command, the actions expected on the corps commander would depend on what the status of these individuals or groups are. And you highlight four scenarios: Enemy forces; units from the same army; units from a different army; and the fourth scenario, unknown groups. And my question to you is: When a commander has, in his area of operations, unknown groups which are not under his command, can you explain, based on your report, what he is expected to do, based on your experience.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander is, in the first place, responsible for his corps, for all the personnel, all the resources and everything that he is doing in the execution of the mission assigned to his corps. Everything else that is outside the corps, regardless of what it may be, if it has no direct impact on the corps's mission, the corps commander, in my view, should have nothing to do with it. If, in the execution of the mission of the corps, anything may happen in the area of responsibility of the corps, that may affect or begin to affect the execution of the corps's mission in any respect and to any extent, the corps commander, depending on what it is - and in this particular case we are talking about groups of foreigners - he must ask himself what it is and, depending on the degree of their influence over the execution of the corps's mission, to that extent he must show interest in the problem and try to deal with it. However, I mention these four scenarios here, which are the most frequent regarding the status of various groups, should unknown groups appear and they still don't have any particular affect on the corps's mission and it is up to the corps commander, once he learns about those groups, to inform the civilian police about them and for them to take the necessary measures. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My next question deals with -- in your report, and I refer specifically to paragraph 638. Can you confirm that what you have just explained is found in paragraph 638 and 639 of your report.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is confirmed in paragraph 638 mostly what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, in paragraph 639 at the end, the last measure, there's a word that attracted my attention where it says amongst the things that the corps commander can be expected to do. You mention, "In consultation with his superior command, take measures proportional to the problems created by these individuals or groups of individuals to ensure that the accomplishment of the mission of the corps will not be hampered." I'm curious about the word "proportional", and can you explain, further, what you mean by this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem, with respect to the presence of foreigners, individuals or groups within the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, their activities, and, as time passes their activities change and, in time, they become more and more conspicuous, more and more noticeable, so that all of their acts, in a certain time period, become increasingly complex and the problem of the conduct of those foreigners in time becomes greater and more complex. To that same extent, this affects the mission of the corps. And with the growth or the increase of the problem of foreigners, and with the degree of threat that they represent to the corps, to that same extent, the corps commander, in order to protect the corps's mission will focus on the problem of foreigners and take certain steps. Or to -- in simpler terms, for as long as those people were engaging in humanitarian people in various locations, and they may have offended somebody or stopped someone in the street, or hit someone, I don't know what other illustrations to use, these are all minor matters which do not directly affect the corps' mission. And the corps commander, therefore, he can say, quite correctly - and I would do the same - those are people doing something for which the civilian police is responsible and I don't have time to bother with them. But at a certain point in time, when these excesses or incidents become so serious as to directly affect the authority and rating of the corps commander and the corps as a whole and the nature of struggle of the corps, then their conduct has palpable affect on the corps' mission. In that case the corps commander must take certain steps to protect himself and his position, his authority and the nature of the struggle of his corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would like to ask you to comment on an answer to a question which was put to General Cordy-Simpson on this issue, and to provide your opinion as to whether this corresponds to your own opinion which you expressed in your report. And the question was as follows: "What do you expect the corps commander to do about crimes committed by people who are not his subordinates?" And the answer which was provided was as follows: "Yes, I understand your question clearly. I think it depends entirely whether he has any influence on that particular organisation which, accordingly, is not part of his subordinates. All he can do is report the matter higher, that there is some force that is behaving outside control in his area. He has no ability because he has no command function over someone who is not under his command. It is a fundamental military principle and one that we certainly, wherever I have been, you have to establish exactly your command relationships with everyone in your area. And I don't want to confuse people, but there is a huge difference in being opcon, operational control, and opcon, operational command. And for me it would be one of the first things I would establish whether forces in my area were opcom to me or not. Now that's easy because I come from an organisation that has been brought up under Staff College trainings and all the rest. It isn't quite so easy in the confused situation that we are talking about in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't believe that if a force is operating which is not under your operational command, there is much you can do when they get out of control." Can you comment, General, on this answer provided by General Cordy-Simpson.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can comment on it, by saying that I agree with his comments to the greatest extent. It is an exhaustive and complete comment. If you want me to comment more specifically on certain points, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, maybe, General, I would like to address the fact that General Cordy-Simpson appears to say that there is not much you can do, whereas you appear to say that there is actually more you can do. How much can you do and what determines what you will or will not do?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that the corps commander can do in such a situation is, once he learns about such groups which are not under his command and within his corps, but are in the area of responsibility of the corps, is to order his security service to pay more attention to this and to collect as much information about them as possible regarding their location, their numbers, who they are, what they are, what they're doing, what their intentions and objectives are and so on. But this is a lengthy process. It's something that cannot be done in an hour or a day or two. To collect intelligence takes time. And that is the kind of measures he can take. That's all he can do. At the same time, he can exchange that information with services in the civilian police if the system is functioning. And of course give the primacy in dealing with that problem to the civilian police because it is part of their competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. There is one concept which was -- which has been raised during this trial on a couple of occasions. The first time I guess it was raised was with General Reinhardt an then again it was raised with General Merdan, deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, and it's an issued call horizontal cooperation. Are you familiar with this term of horizontal cooperation and what does this mean to you, and could that be applied to the issue of foreign fighters in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, horizontal cooperation represents cooperation between two entities at the same level. Or, cooperation of two entities on a particular task, without any relationship of superiority or subordination between them. To be more specific, I will give you an example or two. If the defence line is taken control of by two brigades, and at the point where the left flank of one brigade connects with the right flank of another brigade, these may be two battalions, as lower level units within a brigade. In order to control this point, that could be an example of horizontal cooperation. Those two battalion commanders are cooperating horizontally to be in contact at the point of linkage. This could be raised to the higher level between brigade commanders, or even to corps commanders where they have contact with each other, because the enemy, in executing his mission, is looking for weak points in the enemy's defence. And those weak points are precisely the points where these two units touch. That is an example of horizontal cooperation. Another example could be given with this particular case. When the military security service of the 3rd Corps or the 3rd Corps as such may cooperate horizontally with the civilian police, as the corps is territorially responsible for the area of central Bosnia, there was also the security services centre in Zenica, that is the civilian police which roughly was responsible for the same area of Central Bosnia. So when talking about foreigners, then this concept of horizontal cooperation may be applied between the security service of the 3rd Corps and the civilian police security service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless you have a follow up question, we could break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a very brief question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, I followed you right up until the last three lines and I don't understand the last three lines when you say when talking about foreigners this concepts of cooperation may be applied between security service of the 3rd Corps and the civilian police security service. I don't understand. Can you please explain just this last part.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's simple. In a state, if the overall defence system is functioning and that defence system is comprised of many entities. One of those is certainly the army, the defensive armed force. Another entity is the civilian police, not to mention the entities within the defence system. Then both these two entities within the defence system have to be in the service of the struggle for a single goal and that goal is to defend the state. And all the information available to the civilian police, which might be of use to the 3rd Corps, it is duty-bound to pass on to the security service of the 3rd Corps. And similarly and simultaneously all the information available to the security service of the 3rd Corps or the 3rd Corps as such and which may be of interest to the civilian police, it is duty-bound to pass on to the civilian police. This is an example of horizontal cooperation and exchange of information. Similarly, in America, the CIA and the FBI, the CIA is responsible for the external aspects and the FBI for the internal aspects. And there is a common interest between them. Both of them, both of those organizations exist with a view to achieving the same goal and that is the protection of the United States and they are duty-bound to exchange information amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think we can now have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is 10.32, we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's five seconds to 11.00. Mr. Bourgon, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General when we left just before the break, you provided some clarification with respect to your answer on horizontal cooperation. Now, my question to you is: My understanding, based on your answer, is that horizontal cooperation could be something like cooperation at the same level which exists within an organisation, but cannot exist outside of an organisation. So can you explain whether it is possible to have this concept of horizontal cooperation between a unit of the army and a group which is outside of the army.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, no, it's not possible; however, I won't provide you with any specific examples. But depending on whether a higher level designates a group or an entity, and says that for a given period of time it is necessary for a certain task to be carried out, and then the possibility is given to establish such horizontal cooperation, in such circumstances we can't exclude this possibility, but that's very rare. It's so rare that I'm not even sure that I have ever experienced any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To follow up on your answer, General, I would like to know if horizontal cooperation is possible between a unit of the 3rd Corps and a group of foreign fighters, to be very specific.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, I don't think this is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, in the case of horizontal cooperation, even when it does exist, so I take the example that you raised earlier, that of being two brigade acting side by side, which are units of the 3rd Corps. Who is responsible for the actions of the members of both brigades who are into this mode of horizontal cooperation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The high level, the superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question, General, refers to information we found in the evidence, and you may or may not be aware of this, some witnesses have said that as 3rd Corps units took part in some combat activities, some foreign fighters, known as Mujahedin, as you referred to them in your report, appeared during -- as the combat activities were taking place. What status do these foreign fighters or Mujahedins have in relation to the army?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the initial period and based on all the documents that I have read and up to the time when these foreign combatants started committing serious crimes, which had a direct and immediate influence on the way in which the corps' mission was being carried out, up until that point in time the 3rd Corps commander had no particular obligations in relation to them, apart from doing what we have already spoken about, what we spoke about a while ago. Having obtained information about individuals, about their groups, he should then try to establish horizontal cooperation with the civilian police to identify them, et cetera, et cetera. When their acts started interfering with the corps' mission, then Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the corps commander had to find certain solutions, and had to determine how to act with regard to them in order to accomplish the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I will say my question over again. Maybe I was not very clear. If you were a commander involved in combat activities on the ground, and a group of Mujahedin showed up as the combat activities were going on, and they happened to be shooting in the same direction as you are shooting, basically firing on the same enemy that you are firing on, what -- how do you assess such a situation as a military commander? Are there good sides to it? Are there down sides to it? And how would you react?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such a situation as the 3rd Corps commander -- well, above all I have to address the issue as a man and as a corps commander, in that period of time, not from this perspective 12 years after the events. At that point in time, whoever joined in firing on the enemy together with myself, whoever did this would have been more or less helping me. This would have been welcomed. However, there's another thing. As a corps commander, after one such event, or immediately after the first event or perhaps after the second event, I'd have to ask myself who this group of people were. Are they army members, civilians, something completely different? Why are they here? On the basis of whose instructions, directives and orders are they doing what they're doing? The fact that their acts are helping me instead as the corps commander is one matter. They're helping me to fight an enemy and I'm fighting for my survival, so any assistance is, in that sense, assistance that I would more or less accept. But on the other hand, I would immediately have to take the steps I have mentioned afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Before I follow-up on those steps that you are talking about, I would just like to come back to the combat activities on the ground, and if you were that commander on the ground, not the corps commander, but if you were that commander on the ground and you saw these people showing up during the combat activities, is that only good for you, or can that also be -- have a different affect on your combat activities?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I don't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will try once again. You are a battalion commander and you are involved in combat activities. As you are involved, Mujahedin show up uninvited and unplanned where you are conducting your combat activities. You mentioned earlier that there was a good side to this, because if they are fighting in the same direction or firing their weapons in the same direction, that could be of assistance. Are there also some negative consequences to these people showing up in the middle of your combat activities? Would you like that as a military commander? And how would you react and what would you tell your superior commander after as to what should or should not be done with this group?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is this danger, if I don't know who this group is, the group firing in the same direction that I am at a given point in time or, rather, that my troop are firing in. This does not mean that under other circumstances and at some other point in time this group might not open fire on me, if I don't know the identity of this group. This is a threat. This is a danger that is constantly present for a corps commander let's say for a battalion or brigade commander. However, if this happens, the corps commander has to request that information be obtained about the truth, that is to say he has to request that he be provided with as much information and facts as possible about this group. I mentioned a while ago that he had to find out who they were, what they were, what their real objective was, how many of there were, what they were doing, et cetera. And having obtained that information within the chain of command, it's then his duty to inform his superior. He must submit a request to regulate the status, to define who they are and then to regulate their status. Or, he has to request authorisation for him to deal with it or for the civilian police to deal with it exclusively or for him to help the civilian police to deal with it and, if necessary, to use armed forces to deal with them, to eliminate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, based on your experience - and I would like to follow exactly on what you just mentioned - on the possibility to use armed force to deal with this group, at what point does seeking information become not enough and you need to make -- to take further action, whether it be to fight them, or something else as you mentioned in your report? What's the trigger point where you say: "Information is not enough"?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The trigger point is the point in time when that group starts causing so many problems that they're seriously interfering with the corps' mission. The question then arises, as to the possibility of carrying out the corps' mission, as to the character, the nature of the corps mission. Then the corps commander, if he wants to pursue his mission, has to ask his superior to take certain measures, to deal with their status, or to eliminate them by having recourse to arms; however, on the basis of all of the information that the corps commander would send to the superior -- to his superior -- or having sent all of this information, how his superior will react is a different matter and how he will respond to the corps commander is a different matter. It is possible to have an exchange of correspondence that can go on for a while. That concerns information. But with regard to the use of force, the corps commander should not use force in those circumstances without having previously obtained the authorization of his superior. I can provide you with an example which is perhaps similar. It concerns a case I had in Sarajevo. It might be appropriate for this case. In the course of 1993 I had a problem with two brigades. The 9th Motorised Brigade and the 10th Mountain Brigade. At the head of the 10th mountain brigade there was Tupalovic, Musan, aka Caco. Under the head of the 9th there was Sulejman Imsirevic, but his deputy was Ramiz Delalic, also known as Celo. He was the deputy, but he was in fact the commander. In spite of the fact that he was the deputy, he acted as if he were the commander. Those two brigades, from the beginning of 1993, and from the spring of 1993, really started to show disrespect for the chain of command. Documents were sent from the 1st Corps commander who preceded me then when I assumed that command, documents were sent from me. I sent documents to deal or rather solve the status of the commanders of those brigades or rather of those brigades. However the situation was different. Those two brigades were under my full command. They were part of the organic structure of my corps. And no one else had any rights over them, apart from myself as the corps commander apart from the corps commander. This is not the case when you have foreign combatants. They don't form the part of anyone's structure. I couldn't say that this was a task of the civilian police. In this case, after numerous problems encountered I won't go into them all, we come to the 26th of October, 1993 when I requested, from the supreme commander and from the General Staff and from the president and from the commander of the General Staff, to forward to me a written document authorising me to use armed force to remove two commanders, the deputy of the 9th and the commander of the 10th. In order to place those brigades under my full command again, to integrate them within my chain of command. I didn't want to proceed in this manner without having obtained the document I am referring to. When I received the document the document stated that in cooperation with the civilian police and others, in cooperation with other entities, but naturally I had to accomplish most of the tasks. I was told I could do this. On the 26th of October 1993 I used armed force to remove two commanders and to place two brigades under my full command by using force. In this fight, Sarajevo was encircled. I had to form another circle within that circled around those two brigades. On that occasion, about 20, almost 20 of my policemen from my military police company were killed. Quite a few policemen from the civilian police force were killed. I'm only talking about how serious the problem was. And that actual action I organised, the son of the minister of police died, was killed. As a policeman this shows how serious this was. It was so serious that now, 12 years later, from this perspective, it's difficult to go back to the situation that prevailed at the time and assess it. I was able to do what I did with the two brigades because they were in a small area, because Sarajevo doesn't cover a very large territory, the territory of Sarajevo that was encircled by the Republika Srpska army. I knew the exact locations. They were under command, et cetera. But in the case of this group of people that we are discussing, the situation was different. They were individuals, people scattered throughout the territory of Central Bosnia. They would move around, not in accordance with any particular schedule. They weren't responsible to anyone. They themselves would plan what they would do, et cetera, et cetera. The situation was quite different, and in such a situation the 3rd Corps commander was not in a position to act in the way that I acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. To follow up on this situation, you talked -- you did mention about the serious character of the problem. I'm curious to know whether you had forces available to conduct such combat activities, if there was combat activities, or if you had the forces available, and what information you had on this group, in terms of location, numbers, identity, weapons, ammunition, timings, whatever information you had on those groups before any mission was launched.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about my two brigades? In this case that I have just been telling you about, I have to admit that I had a lot of the information that I required at that time to take such a decision and to carry out that task, to remove those commanders and their followers. Or rather, to place the brigades under my full command again. And I was in a position to act in this way for the reasons I have mentioned. Up until the end of 1992, perhaps up until the spring of 1993, I had some form of contact with their commander or rather with them, and I had enough time to gather all the relevant information that I needed to ensure that I didn't make any mistakes and that I didn't fail. I knew where one of the commanders -- I knew where the commanders were, I knew where the groups of people who supported the commanders were located, et cetera. So on the 26th of October, 1993, in the morning, at five o'clock in the morning, I went into action and as of midnight, with specially prepared units, units that had been prepared over a one-month period, I sent them in certain directions, without anyone's knowledge, to encircle and block all the locations where they were deployed, from the brigade commands to their battalion commands, some company commands, their logistics centres where they had logistics supplies, communication centres, et cetera, et cetera. So at that point in time at five o'clock in the morning when the signal was given everything was in place, we started encircling them we started carrying out an armed attack, but the fight with the commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade continued until the evening. It lasted throughout the day. So a lot of men were killed on both sides. But all of these men were my men, men of the ABiH 1st Corps. And in the evening the commander of the 10th mountain brigade surrendered. He was then eliminated, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, would you have launched this attack without all the information that you had?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is the following. I wouldn't have gone into this action without having obtained the written authorization and an order from the supreme commander from my commander because I requested such authorization from President Izetbegovic. I wanted it to be put down in paper, and I said I would then go into action. If I didn't receive anything in writing from my supreme command, I wouldn't go into action because of the overall political situation. I shouldn't take the initiative to go into action independently, because afterwards, the situation in Sarajevo would have been chaotic and as a result Sarajevo could have imploded from inside without an external attack. An aggressor on the outside could just walk into Sarajevo. It's a very complex issue and it would be necessary to expand on it at length. But I wouldn't have acted without such authorisation and I wouldn't have acted without having sufficient information on these two brigades, on these commanders, on their groups. I wouldn't have acted without having all the information I needed to go into such action.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned a little earlier, General, that the problem related to these brigades had been brought to the attention of the supreme command before by your -- the commander who was in place before you. Now, what I would like to know is, how much time was there between the identification of the problem as these brigades being out of control and the activities that you launched to take them back into control?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that my predecessor, the commander of the 1st Corps, Mustafa Hajrulahovic -- I don't know the exact date but I think it was probably in May or maybe beginning of June. Anyway, around then he sent a document - which exists in the archives of the Army of the Federation Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. today - requesting that the General Staff and the supreme command urgently replace the commander of the 10th mountain brigade, Mustafa Caso [phoen] and Ramiz Delalic, Celo, the deputy commander. And I think that this document contains one or two other names. And we didn't launch the operation before the 26th of October, so you can see, from May until October, which makes it just under five months. If the sending of the document requesting their dismissal was sent in June, but the problem existed even before then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, there is an error. The name on page 40, line 19, it is not Mustafa, Alivocic [phoen], but another name, which I would -- which I will correct in the transcript a little later. Also, there may also be another error in the interpretation when the witness said in line 25: [In English] "We didn't launch the operation before the 26th of October." [Interpretation] I think that the witness did not use the word "operation".

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I would like to continue by asking you, very quickly, what did the VRS around Sarajevo think of what was going on in the city which was besieged, of seeing you fighting your own men? How did the VRS react?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, the interpreter apologises. Failed to switch on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, if you can start your answer over again. There was a technical difficulty.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Sarajevo Romanija Corps of the VRS, which held Sarajevo under total blockade and under siege, at the time, through communication means, which we managed to intercept by tapping and in other ways, reacted by, first of all, wondering what the Balijas, as they usually called members of the ABiH, or the Muslims, what are they doing down there? They keep saying they have nothing, no men, no weapons, yet they're fighting among themselves. So there were comments along these lines. They were surprised. They were astonished. And then at the same time, having learnt about this, to take advantage of the situation, they carried out certain attacks to take advantage of our internal problems and weaknesses, and to benefit from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, was it difficult to obtain the authorization from your president to conduct these activities?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was, to a great extent. I can also take this as an example. That is, when I was talking to President Izetbegovic about this, because I said something like that in connection with the Tribunal here. I think that we need to check the documents in the archives. I think that this was some 20 or so days before the 26th of October, 1993, when I simply didn't know what to do in terms of control and command of my corps. I had an operative group and all the forces of the corps that were defending the city of Sarajevo from within, and two such operative groups with a large number of brigades outside the town of Sarajevo which were defending the territory around the town of Sarajevo, endeavouring from the outside to lift the blockade around the city. The year 1993 was of key significance for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. To give you just an example of the problems that we were having at the time, at the beginning of 1993, when an attack on Azici [phoen] as deputy commander of the corps at the time and who was deciding on the deployment of equipment, a corps of 75.000 men was left with 800 bullets. They didn't have a single bullet in reserve, not to mention a shortage of food, no electricity, no water, no way to prepare food for the army, humanitarian aid wasn't coming, et cetera. So throughout 1993, these enormous problems arose and one might ask why those problems arose, but that would be a different matter. Anyway, the time came when I spoke to President Izetbegovic and said, "I can no longer continue being corps commander until I resolve these problems. Otherwise, please replace me. I will become a regular soldier." His brief answer was, though we had had several prior conversations, he said, was I really serious? I said that I was very serious and I said: "Please put it in writing that I am allowed to use armed force to normalise the situation in the corps and to place everything under my command." His answer then was: "Wait 10 or 15 minutes for me to carry out political preparations." Those were his words. Probably with the other members of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Hercegovina and many other political entities and then you will get a written document. And that is when I started serious preparations for that action, which actually occurred on the 26th of October. Interpreter's correction: 10 to 15 days and not minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. At the time these activities took place, on the 26th of October, can you compare the state of organisation of the 1st Corps with the state of organisation of the 3rd Corps? Which one was more advanced in its organisation and why?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's rather a difficult question. I can speak about my own corps, but to compare the 1st with the 3rd corps and to say which was more organised, perhaps the commander of the General Staff or our superior would be able to answer that question. They were better able to see that. But in any event, I can tell you what my thoughts were. We were more or less comparable.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will try to be a bit more specific, General. When was the 1st Corps created and how long had it been in existence by 26 October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Corps of the ABiH was formed on the 1st of September by the order when all the corpses were formed. We consider the date to be the 1st of September, 1992. And from then on, until the end of 1993, the 1st Corps was constantly in a stage of transformation and reorganisation. This went on continuously. And two days ago, I think, I said here that I believe that the 1st Corps stood on its feet as a corps, as an operational unit at the end of 1993. Only then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in its organisation, did the 1st Corps meet all the difficulties that you describe in your report, those difficulties that were encountered by the 3rd Corps? Did you meet more, less, or the same difficulties as General Hadzihasanovic encountered in setting up the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is impossible to give a generalised answer to say that we were in the same position in every respect. In certain respects, I had a more favourable status and in other respects, the 3rd Corps was in a worse position and vice versa. So I can give you endless examples. If we're talking about food, for instance, the 3rd Corps was in a far more favourable position, because they had a large territory, a large population, and food production was available in the area from which they could feed their units and the corps. However, I, in Sarajevo, in such a small area, with a large population and a large number of soldiers, I had close to 40.000 troops within the city of Sarajevo alone and these had to be fed, et cetera. So every spring, I had to form special companies in each brigade to sow potatoes, onions, et cetera, so that that when there was space somewhere for this to be done, we had to make up for the shortage of food. However, generally speaking, comparing the problems that I was encountering as commander of the 1st Corps and General Hadzihasanovic as commander of the 3rd Corps, I think these were comparable. And if I'm talking about 1993, I think the overall situation was more complex in the 3rd Corps than in the 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, you mentioned a little earlier the difference between what you decided and ended up doing in Sarajevo, and you made a comparison with the situation of the foreign fighters in Central Bosnia. And my question to you would be as follows: From a military standpoint, based on your extensive military experience, which action would be more difficult. To take on, as you did, a brigade with all of the information and the resources and the authorization that you had, or to try and take on a group of foreign fighters, as you describe in your report, without the necessary information in the situation that General Hadzihasanovic was in?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is a rather broad one. I think I understand it, but to avoid a lengthy answer, could you put the question in shorter terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How difficult would it have been if General Hadzihasanovic had wanted to do similar actions as you did in Sarajevo to solve the foreign fighters' problem? How can you compare the two, from a military standpoint?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said "then", that is in 1993, that I would not launch the action to depose two of my brigade commanders without an appropriate decision by the political leadership of the state, I had plenty of reasons why I wouldn't have done that.
