And that is because, after that, the political turmoil in the city of Sarajevo could have climaxed to such a point as to lead to -- lead me into a position when the whole corps would fall apart and Sarajevo would fall from within, as I said a moment ago. And I stand by what I said. That is why I needed such a political decision, which the president probably prepared. And once we completed the action, and despite the number of casualties, the number of our soldiers who were killed, there were no special political consequences. On the contrary, the corps emerged much more powerful and much more stable from this action. Now, let us take the situation of the 3rd Corps commander. These groups of men were not part of the 3rd Corps, and actually, have nothing to do with the 3rd Corps. The 3rd Corps commander doesn't have confirmed and reliable information which he would need and which were essential for him to plan a possible action against those people. So the differences were enormous. Next, these men judging from all the documents I have read and the basis of my knowledge during the war and after the war, everything I have read and heard, when those men appeared, they pretended to be humanitarians, they had plenty of food, they had money, they had clothing, and they would give all of this to the population in certain parts of Central Bosnia. Their probable main goal was for the civilian population to accept them and for them to do well. And that is how, to put it bluntly, they were buying the civilian population. They were buying the attention of the civilian population. And what happened in time, what happened was that as time passed, they were winning more and more attention from the civilians. And let me make my own conclusion, which may not be the correct one, that at some point in time - it's difficult to say whether it was April, May, June or July, 1993 - that a certain number of the civilian population in certain areas more or less equally respected these men as they did their own army, not to mention that certain individuals and groups even had greater feelings for these groups. All of this shows that if the 3rd Corps commander was were to take armed action against those men, without the permission of the political leadership it is highly questionable what the upshot would be. Could he have, as I could have had, internal problems as a result, political problems and problems within the civilian population as well who -- which might have had a negative impact on the overall structure of the 3rd Corps and of course on the 3rd Corps's mission. And this would only benefit the VRS and the HVO. So these are matters that the 3rd Corps commander had to have in mind and he, in fact, did give these matters thought. It was very difficult in those days to take decisions of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, a quick technical question. How big is a detachment?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: A detachment, as a formation, is most frequently used in the territorial defence, the component of the armed forces called the Territorial Defence. And "battalion" is the term used in the army. A battalion is numerically larger than a detachment. A detachment numbers 300 to 500 men and a battalion is about 500 to 700 men. I've just made a comparison between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question, General, is, you are aware -- in your report you mention the creation of the El Mujahid detachment, and this is not in your report, but I would like to have your opinion on this: If they use the word"detachment" with "El Mujahid" would there be a relationship between the number of people that they imagine could be in this unit, such as you say for a detachment, between 300 to 500?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances, the two should be connected. However, under circumstances in which the ABiH army was living and working, this was just a role in principle, in declaration. But in reality there was a very large diversity to the effect that, especially in 1992 and up to a point in 1993 as well, there was a brigade that was called a brigade because the commander appointed himself as commander and was later Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. confirmed as such by the superior because he had to be confirmed because the troops were listening to him and the brigade only had a couple of hundred of men in it. Or up to 1 thou men so there were many such examples. And all brigade in principle had two, three, to 5.000 men, depending on the type of brigade. The same applies to detachment, there they may be called detachments, there were detachments that had only up to 100 men, or a battalion that had 200 or 300 men. So this was the reality in all the corps of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question General deals with your assessment of the situation in respect of the presence of foreign fighters in Central Bosnia. And you highlighted the measures that were taken and that is in your report at paragraph 643, right up until 650. And then your conclusion is at 651, right up until paragraph 662. I would like to have your opinion as to whether General Hadzihasanovic, his assessment of the situation and the measures taken, were that of a reasonable commander in the circumstances at the time.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said most of it in the relevant paragraphs in my report on the basis of the numerous documents I had access to. I think, therefore, that your question, and in answer to that question, I believe that to the greatest possible degree any commander, as commander of the 3rd Corps, would have acted very similarly, if not in an identical way as he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have one more question in respect of taking on the foreign fighters or fighting the foreign fighters. In many occasions during this trial a question was put to witnesses as to whether they had the necessary resources to fight the Mujahedin. Basically, in the terms of saying: How can a corps of more than 30.000 men, is it possible that such a corps did not have the resources to undertake activities to fight the Mujahedin? What would be, one, your opinion on the facts, but also your opinion based on your experience?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, if I may say so, that this is a very good question. Why do I believe that it is a good question? Because many people -- and I don't want to offend anyone -- many lay men who know very little or nothing about the military, many such people just accept examples, for example, here the 1st Corps had 75.000 men. A layman will immediately say, well look, if you have 75.000 men, you can liberate territory and you can reach Belgrade. But this is just a matter of deceiving someone. It is deceptive. Why? Because I as the 1st Corps commander with so many men, real combatants -- what do I men when I say real combatants? I mean somebody who was ready to take a rifle and go into action against the enemy, to kill the men mi or to be killed out of the enemy. Out of those 75.000 men, I don't know whether I had -- well, it's difficult for me to provide you with a real number, but I'm not sure whether I had 10.000 such men out of the 75.000. So as for the other men, you can call them soldiers, that was the case in the ABiH. And in all corps, you just use the term "soldier". But this soldier didn't have a uniform. He didn't have a rifle. And he was entrenched at the line, two metres underground, and he would just observe and occasionally when it was his shift he would be given a rifle and, if there was a serious attack launched by the enemy, then serious problems would immediately arise because many men weren't prepared to wait for the enemy. When the enemy headed in his direction with a rifle, I wouldn't want to be too critical here, but at the same time I would like to explain a certain situation. Why am I telling you about this? At any point in time, at some point in time the 3rd Corps commander in mid 1993 and I think that this is contained in my report, had a defence line that was almost 300 kilometres long, facing the Republika Srpska army. At the same time, When the lines were established he had about -- he had a line of about 100 kilometres facing the HVO. So let's say that the defence lines were about 400 kilometres long, roughly speaking. If we say -- according to the rules, 8 eight metres between two soldiers let's say there is even ten. Sometimes it is denser. Sometimes it is not so dense. But if you have a soldier every ten metres, that means if you have a 400-kilometre long defence line, the corps commander needs 400.000 -- needs 40.000 soldiers just to man the defence lines. But he often had fewer men. I'm not sure whether he ever had more than 40.000 men at any point in time. That's one thing. But if we take into consideration the case that I have mentioned, well in the 3rd Corps the situation was no better, if it was the same as in the 1st Corps and if we assume that it's necessary to attack such men who are ready to die if someone threatens them, then the question is: How many such men did the 3rd Corps commander have? He had very few such men. And the question now is, if such a situation arose, would it be better to keep such can you remember age us soldiers in reserve in the direction of Maglaj, in the direction of Travnik, Turbe, Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, to prevent the HVO from descending above, on Vlasic, to prevent the Republika Srpska descending into Travnik, wouldn't it have been better to have them at critical locations? And critical locations assessed by the command, and the commander. I don't know if I've been sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would like to move on by asking you a few questions, still on the issue of foreign fighters. Now, these were questions that were put to General Reinhardt. And I would like to, in as few words as possible, say whether you agree or you don't and why. The first question was: "In your area of responsibility, there are soldiers of foreign origin. If these soldiers are prepared to fight for the same cause as yourself, are fighting for, but and if, on the other hand, they are unwilling to be placed fully under your command, but preferred to have a rather loose horizontal relationship with you and your troops, then that would be an awkward situation, I presume, for a commander?" And General Reinhart's response was: "Sir, this is a very bad situation because, as we discussed before, unity of command in an area of responsibility is a key factor." What do you think of the response?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I share General Reinhart's opinion almost fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And another question was: "So if you are faced with this situation, when assuming command, the first thing you would do is to try to stop this situation as soon as possible." General Reinhart responded: "Yes, sir, to stop or to solve it. It might be that there's a possibility to solve it rather than stopping it." Your opinion, please.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that in this case too, General Reinhardt was quite clear. And I absolutely agree with that position he expressed. When General Hadzihasanovic assumed his duties, when he found out about the existence and the problem concerning these groups, he kept insisting on dealing with this problem, on solving the problem. Numerous documents bear witness to the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, in his response, General Reinhardt did not address one part of the question which was: "When assuming command, the first thing you would do is to try to stop this situation." Do you agree that when assuming command of the 3rd Corps, the first thing that General Hadzihasanovic should have done was to stop this situation as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that General Reinhart was speaking in general terms. He wasn't referring to any specific dates. As far as I know the problem of foreign groups wasn't a matter of attention when the 3rd Corps commander assumed his duties. This is a problem that arose later on. But General Reinhardt was speaking about such things in general terms and I wouldn't agree with what you have just focussed on, although perhaps in my previous answer I said that I did agree. But when you said, if there is a problem, if there are problematic groups and when the corps commander assumes his duty, is that the first thing he would do? No. I would not agree with that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question that I would like to ask your opinion on is the following. Again a question put to General Reinhardt. "If you accept presence of forces that are not fully integrated in your army, without forcing them to accept your command fully and permanently, do you also accept -- by acquiescing to the situation, do you also accept or assume responsibilities for their acts and conduct, especially or even in situations in which they would take independent action that you have not ordered or, in any way, promoted?" And General Reinhart's answer was: "Sir, this is my understanding of the situation." Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's a very broad question and it contains many details. The following is at issue. A group appeared which attempted in one way or another to join in certain combat action, which the 3rd Corps commander welcomed at one point in time. The question is whether they were doing this in sufficient coordination with the 3rd Corps, or rather in accordance with certain guidelines or were they acting haphazardly on their own initiative? That's one issue. Regardless of how this takes place, the corps commander is only responsible for his men who are an organic part of the 3rd Corps. And he is responsible only for the chain of command, for himself, his deputy, and for all the soldiers down to the very last soldier who are registered in the mobilisation documents of the municipal defence secretariat and who are registered and who have been assigned to one of the units of his corps, or rather to his corps as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you General I'm curious about one part of your answer where you say that: "Which the 3rd Corps commander welcomed at one point in time." I'm just curious, because this seems to be somewhat different from what you said earlier. Did you see any evidence, in all the material that you saw that at any point in time General Hadzihasanovic welcomed any assistance from those foreign fighters?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the issue which was raised in this question, that's my previous question, if I try to be more precise and focus, the question was something like this: If you have forces that are not integrated in your army and you don't force them to accept your command, then you accept responsibility for whatever they do. And General Reinhardt said: This is my understanding of the situation. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. A minute ago I described the situation that I, as the 1st Corps commander was in, in Sarajevo, and I described what I had experienced and what I finally did, from the time that this commenced in the spring of 1992 -- I apologise, in the spring of 1993 or at the beginning of 1993, I told you what had to be done in order to do what was done on the 26th of October, 1993. Everything was done. Everything was attempted. But these units were my units and I had to do that. I had to. That's a huge difference. Sarajevo was a small area. My situation in Visoko and Olovo was quite different. The situation I had in Furcin [phoen] was quite different. In territory outside the town of Sarajevo. There could have been all sorts of things, but I was responsible for my units in Visoko and Olovo and Tarcin. If we have such a situation, responsibility is one thing, or rather temporal authorisation for action taken by, for example, one group. A group accomplishing a task in the interests of the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because as I have said, subconsciously this might suit the corps commander or not because they're firing in the same direction that the corps commander, or rather his troops are firing in. But this doesn't mean that he is responsible, that he has responsibility. But if they commit a crime and the commander finds out about it, that's another matter. It is his obligation to take measures to deal with the crimes and to inform the institutions that are responsible to process those crimes. So this is the same responsibility that each and every citizen of a state has. If a citizen sees in the street that a crime is committed, a criminal offence, then the citizen has the obligation of picking up the phone and informing the relevant institution, an institution that is responsible for processing the crime. And this is the case with the corps commander as well. The situation should have been better. These men should have been united and this was subsequently done, for these problems -- because of these problems, because that's a process. It is impossible to deal with such a situation even now, or I don't know in how many weeks or in how many months. This is a process. Because the situation is so specific, that it's quite simply very impossible to clarify it. You need a lot of time to clarify the situation, who knows when we'll be very clear about everything, especially with regard to these foreign combatants. Who knows when this point will be reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question, General, is another question which was put to General Reinhardt and it goes as follows: If you, in your area of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. responsibility, are confronted with forces that are not integrated in your command, that have a sort of independent existence, and you acquiesce in that situation, does it also engage your criminal responsibility if they commit, within their activities, within their independent activities, certain crime? Now, General Reinhardt is not a lawyer, but the question was put to him and I know you're not a lawyer and I'm just asking you nevertheless for your opinion on this question, and that was: Does it also engage your criminal responsibility if they commit, within their activities, within their independent activities, certain crimes, because General Reinhardt said, his answer was: "I would be responsible, criminally accountable."

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning, General Reinhardt said, that's how the question was formulated, "if the 3rd Corps was in a conflict with those groups," that's how the question started. At the very beginning the question is whether the 3rd Corps was in a conflict with those groups, or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General I'll have to start the question over again, because I think there may be -- may have been a problem with the interpretation. The question was as follows: If you -- in your area of responsibility, there are forces that are not integrated in your command, that have a sort of independent existence and you acquiesce in that situation, does this engage your criminal responsibility if they commit, within their activities, within their independent activities, certain crimes? General Reinhardt said: "I would be responsible, criminally accountable."

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may ask a different sort of question, then I could ask whether General Hadzihasanovic is responsible. In this case, as in the case of the group you've mentioned -- for the HVO as well because the HVO was also in his zone of responsibility. So my question would be: Would he also be responsible for the HVO? General Hadzihasanovic would have the same responsibility he had towards the HVO, towards those groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I have one last question with the Mujahedin and with what you said in your report when you were talking about the various measures that were taken. And this deals with an order which was received from the Supreme Command Staff to send the Mujahedin to Mount Igman, to report to a unit or to disarm them. And you say at paragraph 648 that General Hadzihasanovic informed his superiors that it would not be possible to disarm the Mujahedin, as this would amount to opening a third front. And he attempted to have the order modified. Now, my question relates to the order itself, from the Supreme Command. Do you know which document I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How would you qualify this document, which is sent from the supreme command to General Hadzihasanovic? Was it a formal order? Was it something else? And how should General Hadzihasanovic have reacted to this document? In the way he did, was it appropriate in the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been speaking about how risky it was for the 3rd Corps commanders to do anything on his own initiative because of the consequences of such an act. The document you are referring to is in fact one of a series of measures taken by the 3rd Corps commander to deal an solve the problem of those foreigners. The superior command, if it was to issue an order, in the sense that it should be sent to Mount Igman, in the sense if they weren't sent to Igman they should be disarmed that's what it states in the document as far as I know, if the supreme command was to do this, they should have issued an order in a completely different manner, not in this manner. The document I have examined is in fact - and I have to tell you what my opinion of the document is - it is in fact a formal, an official document, although it fulfils all the legal conditions that an order has to fulfil. The document just says, "Send them to Igman and if you don't disarm them." The corps commander doesn't know how many men there are, nor does he know where they're located, nor does he know how to do this. And they probably didn't ask the corps commander whether he had any reserve forces who could carry out the task and I already said what it meant if you had 75.000 soldiers and I've already mentioned how many real combatants there were, combatants who were ready to fight. And secondly, an order from the General Staff couldn't be forwarded to the corps commander without involving the civilian police, because this was primarily a task for the civilian police and only then for the 3rd Corps commander. If the General Staff really wanted to do what was stated in official terms in the order -- and I apologise, but this task, since it concerns men who are not part of the ABiH, or who are not part of the 3rd Corps, this action should be led by the civilian police with the assistance of the 3rd Corps. In Sarajevo, the situation I had was completely different. It was the reverse. I was in charge of the action with the assistance of the civilian police, because these brigades were my brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. One last question. Also with this order, -- and you discussed this in your report, I cannot find the exact paragraph, but would you expect the corps commander to abide by all the orders he gets from the Supreme Command Staff, or is it different for a corps commander that, on the contrary, you expect him to discuss whether the order is possible and whether the order is in line with the accomplishment of the mission in his assessment?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: One character that characterised the chain of command in the ABiH is that numerous orders were issued. And the preconditions for carrying out most of those orders didn't exist. I think that I said at one point in time that occasionally there would be a sort of hyper production of orders, too many orders were issued. Perhaps I was in such a situation and I issued such orders to my subordinates, but that meant that there was a desire to liberate the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina as soon as possible and to put an end to the war as soon as possible, et cetera, et cetera. And reality wasn't borne in mind. One didn't bear in mind the possibility of carrying out the order. And in our military documents it is stated quite clearly, the following fact is quite clearly stated and emphasised. When a superior issues an order to a subordinate, he has to know all the relevant facts, all the elements that he needs to know in order to issue an order so that that order can be carried out completely. And a day or two ago, I think I mentioned the situation when the 3rd Corps was formed, General Hadzihasanovic was appointed as the corps commander and was immediately issued two orders, to liberate the entire zone of the corporation and to participate in lifting the blockade of Sarajevo. It is not only that he didn't carry out those orders at the time, he didn't carry them out right up until the end of the war. Who knows whether he could have ever carried them out. I have just mentioned this as an example in response to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General after the break we will address the issue which is at paragraph 743 of your report, and that is the events which allegedly took place in the elementary school and the blacksmith shop in Mehurici. If I may ask General that you review this section of the report so report so that we have enough time to cover all aspects of this section. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think it is time for the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will resume at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, we will now look at the paragraph 743 and others of your report which is a section called the events which allegedly took place in the elementary school an the blacksmith shop. And my first question that I would like to ask is: If I look at paragraphs 755 of your report - sorry, 756 - you establish in this paragraph 3 scenarios and I take it that these scenarios refer to or three categories, sorry, the first one being prisoners of war, the second one being persons detained because they are suspected of having committed a criminal act, and you also talk about subordinates detained by order of the commander. Now, I would like to ask you a few questions on these paragraphs, which I believe shed some light on the situation. Let me begin with the subordinates which are -- who are detained by order of a commander because they were punished and they received either a prison or a detaining -- or they were detained. You say in your report that every brigade is expected to have a detention facility, I think you used the word "detention barracks." Can you explain exactly what are the responsibilities of all the brigade commanders in respect of setting up detention facilities for their own soldiers who are disciplined.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each brigade commander is obliged in accordance with the location of the brigades, where the brigade is living and performing its duties and mission, if it is in peacetime or in wartime. If no space is provided, which is called a detention facility, to detain his subordinates who make a disciplinary offence or violation, in peacetime conditions, that detention facility is usually common to a large territory and is common for all brigades. However, as war was a specific situation which placed all the brigades in a specific situation, no such facilities exist and then the brigade commanders, in accordance with their own particular circumstances, if they are housed in stationary facilities, can set aside a room or a premise and, by a certain document, proclaim it as a detention facility. If the brigade is in the field, then that same brigade may find a wooden hut, or even a tent in the middle of a field can be put up, as I have myself done, and put a table and chair in the tent and the subordinate, who has been sanctioned is placed in that tent with a military policeman standing guard outside. So that is the way each brigade commander would act.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, considering that, as you mentioned earlier, you had 30 brigade if not more in the 1st Corps, does that imply that there were 30 detention facilities for the soldiers of your own corps? That's my first question. The second question is, did you know where these detention facilities were?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the fact that I had so many units doesn't mean to say that I had to have so many detention facilities. These detention facilities is something decided upon by the brigade or unit commander. It is formed when necessary and it can be abolished if it is unnecessary, such a detention facility. So there is no need, in wartime or even in peacetime. In peacetime usually there exists such a facility for a wider area because it is assumed that someone will always be in detention. However, in wartime conditions, you don't have to have such a facility non-stop. And your second question, I never enquired really, nor did I request to know exactly where each of the detention facilities was situated. I didn't know where most of them were. I may have known of some.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question deals with the end of paragraph 757 when you say that, "depending on the availability of a facility or the duration of the punishment of detention or imprisonment that was imposed, subordinates could be transferred to a military prison." Can you provide further information on this aspect.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite. That is something that is applied in wartime conditions, because previously I spoke about peacetime conditions. So in wartime, if we have the preconditions to group people together, then it is always desirable for several reasons. One of the reasons being, among other things, that it is normal to expect that the treatment of all prisoners, regardless of which category they belong to, that the treatment at a higher territorial level will be better, though this should not be the rule. But for objective reasons that I referred to a moment ago, if my brigade commander doesn't have any other possibility except to set up a tent in the middle of a field and there is such a detention facility 50 kilometres away in Sarajevo or in Zenica, some sort of central facility where the conditions are much better, then it is better to put them there. Otherwise, they cannot be expected to be given equal treatment. A second reason that makes this always desirable is to relieve lower levels of command of the obligations and duties which, in relation to the brigade's mission, may be of secondary significance. If the brigade commander issues a punishment of 15 or 30 days of detention, it would be desirable for such a person to be moved to a detention facility at a higher level. When he completes his term he joins the unit again. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. This is just -- these are just some of the reasons why this is desirable.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me move on, General, to the -- the issue of members of the enemy who are detained as a result of the armed conflict. Something like prisoners of war. You mentioned that these persons can be kept in detention until the end of the conflict, or until they are exchanged. Who decides whether they will be kept until the end of the conflict or whether they will be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Due to the very fact that prisoners of war are a consequence of combat, those same prisoners of war enjoy the status of a prisoner of war for one basic reason, and that is that they shouldn't be on the other side and should not fire at me, if I am the party that has captured them and placed them in this status of prisoners of war. And whoever captures them also decides how long they will hold them, the maximum being until the end of the conflict or the war. The aim being to prevent them from opening fire at me or my forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the third category, General, you referred to are those persons who are detained because they are suspected of having committed a criminal act. Who are these persons and who would detain them?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two potential categories of people in that group. The main category are prisoners of war. From among the ranks of the prisoners of war, if there is a possibility that some of them may have committed criminal offences, then the superior, through his security service and police, can retain such a person up to 72 hours in some sort of a detention facility, upon which it is his obligation to institute criminal proceedings against such persons through the competent military court. If that is not done, that category of people will either be released or they can be returned to the status of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the second -- you mentioned two potential categories. I take it this is one, and what about the second category?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second category would consist of all those people that one may hear about or assume or learn about and then the initiative is taken to institute criminal liability, who may not be currently present as prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, let me move on to the end of paragraph 757 where you then go on to say that: Civilians may be accommodated in a facility for safety reasons. Which civilians are we talking about? And what is the justification for this?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about a situation such as, for example, in a particular area there might be combat action. And then that area is swept up in combat. In that same area, there may be a certain number of civilians. And due to the overall development of the combat situation in that region, due to actions taken by the enemy to make a breakthrough, deep within the territory of the defend error the enemy may have already been infiltrated into the defender's ranks or for some other reasons, such as the existence of these groups of foreigners in the area, et cetera, in a part of the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps and many other reasons could be listed. The a unit commander may, and it is even desirable, depending okay his own assessment of the overall situation to channel the civilian population, gather them together to have greater supervision over the civilian population with a view to preventing any untoward events which might happen and which might be taken by someone -- a measure that might be taken by somebody against those civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on, General, to paragraph 758 of your report, where you mention three basic levels of responsibility in relation to the handling of prisoners of war, and you say that there are the capture level, the holding level, and the area level. Is this something that is -- comes from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or is this something that is based on practice over time? Can you explain those three levels?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that both is applicable, but if you were to ask me which regulations I relied on, I couldn't give you the source. I would need time. But I touched upon this issue partly in my previous answer. The level at which a capture is made is very important. When speaking about potential inappropriate treatment of prisoners, this is a crucial issue. And it is certainly important to see at what level the prisoners were captured, were they at the level of a platoon, a company, battalion, or brigade. Who was the first to establish contact with the prisoners? After that comes the greater or lesser chance of inappropriate treatment of prisoners of war. Then the level of holding prisoners of war is something that I have already described. It's not the same if you keep prisoners of war in conditions available in the field or in a regional area where, in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps there was such a facility that is the KP Dom in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question, General, is whether this transfer, if I may use this word, from the capture level to the holding level to the area level, is this an obligation, or is this a military -- I hate to use the word -- operational way to deal with prisoners of war? And why are prisoners of war channeled from the capture, to the holding, to the area level?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a simple reason for this. I can give you a brief example from my own experience. When heading towards a combat assignment, when it is normal to expect that there may be prisoners of war, I always insisted that my assistant for security be always near at hand, that is for him to have, along his chain of command, lower level officers in the operations group, brigade command, and battalion command. So that all the police forces at those levels be mutually connected so that if a commander reports to me from the front line that, shall we say, a group of enemy soldiers has been captured, my main concern was that my security service should reach those prisoners of war as soon as possible and to collect them and take them away from the front line into the rear. The reason being that the greatest problems arise precisely then, when the soldiers are on the front lines and when, during combat activities, people are angry, nervous, many -- depending on whether there were many casualties within one's own ranks simply cannot control themselves. And such people can often commit very serious offences. And that was my main motive for pulling the people out, after which the security service knows what their duties are with respect to the 72 hours detention, to collect information and, after that, they are immediately transferred to the regional level or the central prison in Sarajevo that we had, a similar category of prison as the KP Dom in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At paragraph 762, you provide a number of actions which could be expected to take place, whether these, of course depending on the circumstances, and then you say, "directed by or with the knowledge of the corps commander." Where does the foremost responsibility lie, in terms of taking these actions with regards to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say who has the greatest responsibility. The chain of command is most responsible in the case of prisoners of war. From the time they are captured, from the time that POWs are captured up until the time that they are placed in certain satisfactory conditions, a certain process has to be followed. This process can't be carried out by an individual. It's the chain of command that is in charge of this process. If you ask me who is most responsible for the overall processing of POWs and for the status of POWs, it's the chain of command. As you go up the chain of command, the level of responsibility increases. But everyone has to have full responsibility at their own level when it comes to the treatment of POWs and when it comes to their status.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me move on to the issue of interrogation. And is it allowed, when a unit captures prisoners of war, to interrogate them in order to gain some intelligence?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's allowed or not, but that's something that I did. I believe that it should be allowed. And I think it is allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if someone is a prisoner of war, is there information that a prisoner of war should give and nothing more? Or can the prisoner of war say everything he wants?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: A POW has to provide key information concerning himself, his name, place of birth, his rank, if he had a status in his own army; he has to provide this essential information. Anything additional is for the POW to decide whether he should provide information about such things. But whoever interrogates a POW can't use force in order to obtain anything from the POW that the POW does not want to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And looking at the responsibilities of a corps commander, in respect of the handling of prisoners of war, based on your answers in your report, what should a corps commander do in respect of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: A corps commander has to do the following: All the legal regulations on POW status, all the legal regulations on POWs have to be respected so that everyone in the chain of command are aware of the regulations. Everyone has to be aware of the regulations. The regulations have to be provided to everyone in the chain of command. That's one thing. Secondly, he must ensure that additional education and training is provided given that there are already educated officers who, in certain circumstances have direct contact with the POWs. There are the people guarding the POWs, who are keeping the POWs, who have contact with the POWs, et cetera, et cetera. So it's necessary at intervals to inform the chain of command of those documents and additional training has to be provided. And then the corps commander has to make sure that through his assistant for security, and in the military police and others, he has to ensure his assistant for security takes upon himself the major part of responsibility with regard to the status of POWs. And finally the corps commander has to ensure that within the chain of command those who must frequently deal with the status of the POWs are controlled. One has to control how the legal regulations governing the status of POWs are being respected and to what extent they're being respected. I think that those would be the main tasks of a corps commander when it comes to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you expect, General, to see the corps commander visit the detention facilities at various places in his area of responsibility, first in peacetime and in wartime?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Detention units in prison facilities, whether in peacetime or wartime, one never really a matter of focus. This was just one of a series of issues and in the chain of command in accordance with the regulations, within the chain of command these issues should have been dealt with. The corps commander would very rarely, in peacetime and even more rarely in wartime have the occasion to visit and to control detention facilities. It's not something to be excluded. A corps commander can do anything. But in such complex wartime conditions, this is not something that a corps commander would have paid that much attention to, nor would he have spent a lot of time on such an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, when General Reinhardt testified, some questions were put to him concerning the issue of prisoners of war and persons detained. And one of the questions which was put to him was. I will read you the question and his answer and I would like you to comment on it. This is about prisoners of war in general and civilian prisoners in general. "Are there circumstances, in the case of Bosnia, that make the responsibility of a commander even more pressing and more important in this field? I mention interracial or interreligious character, civil war aspects, he have briefly discussed the inexperience of troops, new soldiers, are these factors" - sorry - "are these factors that also increase, so to speak, the responsibility of a commander?" An General Reinhart's answer was: "I think it increases his responsibility." And I would like to have your opinion on this.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree with General Reinhart's opinion for the following reason. A corps commander has one single duty that is indivisible. He has a responsibility that one shouldn't say that, because of the conflict between the Croats and Bosniaks this increases his responsibility. He is not the cause of such a conflict. The corps commander is not the cause of such a conflict. And secondly, a corps commander throughout his zone of responsibility had a mixed population in all parts of the territory. Croats and Bosniaks. Although there was an open conflict in Zenica that commenced in 1993 there were a lot of Croats there and very few Croats left and moved out of Zenica. What does this mean? If you were to pay attention to where there was a Bosniak, in particular building or where there were Croats in particular buildings, or in Central Bosnia, well the entire Central Bosnian areas like a leopard's skin, there is a Bosniak village and then a Croat village. The situation is impossible. That would have been impossible. Had the corps commander paid attention to such issue, he would have become involved in -- if he had become involved in dealing with such a problem, he would have become totally lost and the corps mission Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which was facing the Republika Srpska army would have been sidetracked. However, I wouldn't say that what you have mentioned had no influence at all, naturally it's a very serious question and something that the commander must bear in mind. But in this case, in this specific case, the 3rd Corps commander -- in 1993, in the zone of responsibility, whether the conflict between Bosniaks and Croats couldn't have acted in this way. It was impossible because of that situation -- because of the situation. It was above the level of the 3rd Corps commander. Given the situation with the HVO, you can't say that the 3rd Corps commander had increased responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now I have another question which was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I thought I could work until 2.00 p.m., that was my mistake. I will have time for one last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, in the binders you have beside you, your binders that you brought from Sarajevo, did you find a lot of measures which were taken either by General Hadzihasanovic or by his subordinate commanders to ensure that his duty would be respected; that is, his duty to prevent and punish and to fulfil his duty as a commander. If you look at your binders, how many of those measures do you have beside you, or how many binders of measures do you have beside you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw numerous documents that concerned the measures that you have just mentioned. Most of the documents in these binders are entitled: Measures. There are 6 binders, from 1 to 6, and the title given to these binders is "measures". As I was in a similar situation to that of the 3rd Corps commander, I can't say that I'm sure that I issued this many documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would just like to have one quick comment on the conclusion, which was made by General Reinhardt where he said: "Having seen so many documents which prove that General Hadzihasanovic did not only issue orders but also went through the whole circle of making sure that the perpetrators were treated legally, according to the law, I would change. And I have changed my attitude, saying that he only initiated the first step and did not do the other steps. Obviously he did this." My question is: On the basis of this opinion, and all the measures you have seen in the material provided to you, did General Hadzihasanovic fulfil all of his responsibilities as a corps commander in Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat what I said a while ago. I said I was in a very similar situation to the situation that the 3rd Corps commander was in. And also given the fact that I believe that I have very good knowledge of the overall political and military situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the course of 1993 and throughout the war, I read through numerous documents that I was provided with, had a brief look at some of them, consulted numerous and diverse sources. I spoke to a sufficient number of people whom I considered to be cleverer than I am, in order not to overestimate or underestimate certain things. If I try to go back to 1993 now, I must admit that I don't know whether I would have been in a position to do anything better, and I personally don't believe that there is some other general, from any army in the world, I don't believe there is any politician or anyone else who would have acted in a way that was better than the way in which General Hadzihasanovic acted as 3rd Corps commander. And I have one more sentence I would like to say. I am fully persuaded that, given the example that the 3rd Corps commander provided, given his knowledge his courage his ability, et cetera, given his moral nature, his fight for Bosnia-Herzegovina and everything that is specific to Bosnia-Herzegovina, given all of these factors, given the work he carried out, he quite certainly prevented, in my opinion, far worse things from happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Central Bosnia. And everything of a negative nature, because it was ugly and it happened in his zone of responsibility is something that was the result of certain objective factors and if everything had been ideal, that would have been the best solution. But unfortunately, there was nothing ideal at the time. There is no adequate word that one could use to describe the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, I wanted to finish at five to, but I failed to do so. But thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, unfortunately you will have to remain here for a few days, unless you'll be leaving for a few days, but in any event you will be returning on Tuesday, next Tuesday and the hearing will commence at 2.15 p.m. I invite everyone to attend the hearing on Tuesday at 2.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 29th day of March, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
